summary: Kawabata took the title of his 1933 essay "Eyes in Their Last Extremity" (末期の眼) directly from Akutagawa's 1927 suicide note, "A Note to a Certain Old Friend." After quoting the passage where Akutagawa writes that nature looks more beautiful to eyes facing death, Kawabata countered that suicide is never, under any circumstances, a form of enlightenment. Scholarship on modern Japanese literature treats the two texts as a pair split apart over art and death.

In 1931, while a Japanese translation of Ulysses was underway, Kawabata published "Crystal Fantasies" (水晶幻想), testing stream-of-consciousness technique in Japanese prose. Scholarship on modern Japanese literature links this experiment from his New Sensationist period directly to Kawabata's reading of Joyce.

Dazai read Akutagawa voraciously as a teenager and was deeply shaken by Akutagawa's 1927 suicide. In 1935 and 1936 he wrote directly to the prize judges, petitioning for the Akutagawa Prize, and those letters survive in his collected correspondence.

When Kawabata, judging the first Akutagawa Prize, wrote a review faulting Dazai's way of life over his story "Gyakko" (逆行), Dazai published "To Yasunari Kawabata" in October 1935 to rebut him publicly. The following year he sent that same man a letter petitioning for the prize.

In his 1945 novel Regret at Parting (惜別), Dazai cast Zhou Shuren — the future Lu Xun — as his protagonist during the character's years at the Sendai Medical School. He wrote it after reading source material including Lu Xun's own memoir "Mr. Fujino," and the record also notes that the novel was commissioned by the Japanese Literary Patriotic Association within the framework of Greater East Asia cultural policy.

The narrator of No Longer Human invokes Dostoevsky's Crime and Punishment by name, asking why crime and punishment sit side by side as if they were antonyms. In Dazai's method of building the confessional mode around guilt, Dostoevsky is a reference point named explicitly within the text itself.

Just after Japan's defeat, the twenty-year-old Mishima visited Kawabata in Kamakura and showed him his manuscripts; on Kawabata's recommendation, "Cigarette" appeared in the magazine Ningen in 1946, launching Mishima's debut in the postwar literary world. The two exchanged letters until 1970, and that correspondence has been collected in book form.

In his 1955 A Novelist's Vacation (小説家の休暇), Mishima wrote that half of Dazai's character flaws could have been cured by cold rubdowns and a regular routine, rejecting Dazai's literature outright. In his 1963 memoir My Wandering Years (私の遍歴時代), he recorded telling Dazai to his face, at the one meeting between them, that he disliked his writing.

In February 1967, Abe and Mishima joined Kawabata and Jun Ishikawa in issuing a joint statement protesting the suppression of scholarship and the arts under China's Cultural Revolution. It is a record of two men with diametrically opposed political positions putting their names to the same document.

Mishima scholarship has repeatedly discussed his novels of the artist's self-consciousness and the destruction of beauty as descendants of Thomas Mann's Death in Venice and Tonio Kröger. The passages that translate the concept of the European Bildungsroman into classical Japanese vocabulary are cited as the basis for that comparison.

Mishima scholarship treats the Apollonian-Dionysian opposition in The Birth of Tragedy as the skeleton of his aesthetics. It is the standard reading that his physical training after traveling to Greece, and the theory of the body in Sun and Steel, are explained on the basis of that reading.

Abe's device of placing a nameless character under an unexplained condition is a standard item that international criticism sets alongside Kafka, and his work from "The Wall — S. Karma's Crime" onward has been read within that lineage. Because no specific document can pin down a statement by Abe himself about reading Kafka, this is recorded one level lower.

In February 1967, Kawabata and Abe joined Jun Ishikawa and Mishima in issuing a joint statement protesting the suppression of scholarship and the arts under China's Cultural Revolution. It is a moment when two writers, wholly different in generation and method, put their names to the same document.

Abe's early-1940s poetry and his first novel, At the Marker of a Road That Has Ended (終りし道の標に), are treated as products of the period when he was reading Rilke. The point where his early, idea-driven style of questioning being and things gives way to the later, dry, premise-driven fiction is explained together with that reading.

There is no record of direct contact between the two. This map places them close together because their methods overlap: each confines a character stripped of name and history within a single condition, then pushes the novel or play through to the end on that condition alone.

The two are widely discussed as colleagues who divided the experimental axis of postwar Japanese literature between them and stood on the same side in political statements as well. The recollection that Oe repeatedly named Abe as a senior writer deserving of the Nobel Prize is passed down through several dialogues, but since it cannot be pinned to a specific primary document, it is recorded at the scholarly-consensus level.

Kawabata's 1968 Nobel lecture, "Japan, the Beautiful, and Myself," connected his own work to the lineage of medieval Zen and waka poetry. In his 1994 lecture "Japan, the Ambiguous, and Myself," Oe quoted that title while changing a single word, and countered that it was a self-definition that papered over the fact that modern Japan was torn between the West and Asia.

The way Oe repeatedly built up a village in a Shikoku valley across multiple works is repeatedly discussed as modeled on Faulkner's Yoknapatawpha County. Oe himself has also placed Faulkner at the center of his own reading, but since the document containing that statement cannot be pinned down, this is recorded one level lower.

In his 1994 Nobel lecture "Japan, the Ambiguous, and Myself," Oe quoted the resolution the Irish Senate presented to Yeats in 1923 and held it up as a position he wished to follow. The title of the trilogy he announced as his final long work, The Flaming Green Tree (燃えあがる緑の木), is also taken from a poem by Yeats.

Scholarship on postwar Japanese literature treats the two writers as a pair standing at opposite poles on the emperor and the postwar Constitution. Mishima moved toward rejecting the postwar order and staging an uprising directed at the emperor, while Oe pushed the defense of postwar democracy and Article 9 of the Constitution through both his novels and his reportage.

Hsia's A History of Modern Chinese Fiction (1961) placed Chang, who took marriage negotiations and property as her axis, into the canon alongside the mainstream after Lu Xun, which took enlightenment and the critique of national character as its axis. Subsequent scholarship has repeatedly contrasted the two as diverging directions on the question of what modern Chinese fiction should write about.

During her stay in Hong Kong in the 1950s, Chang translated Hemingway's The Old Man and the Sea into Chinese and wrote the translator's preface herself. It was one of the translation jobs supported by the United States Information Service, and this period of translation work was the condition of her livelihood before she emigrated to the United States.

There is no record of direct contact between the two. This map places them close together because, after going into exile, both spent their lives moving between two languages, translating and rewriting their own work over and over. Chang's history of revising "The Golden Cangue" repeatedly in both Chinese and English is one example.

There is no record of direct contact between the two. This map places them close together on the shared ground that both cast their female characters not as observers of a family's history but as agents who calculate and manage land, property, and marriage, narrating the shifts of class in modern East Asia through them.

In his apprentice years, Manto began by translating Russian short stories into Urdu, and scholarship on Urdu literature has repeatedly treated his short stories — which strip away commentary and leave only the scene — within the lineage of Chekhov. Whether he translated Chekhov's own work directly cannot be confirmed bibliographically, so this is recorded one level lower.

In his 1936 address "The Purpose of Literature," given at the founding conference of the All India Progressive Writers' Association, Premchand formulated the position that literature must serve a social purpose. Manto did not follow that manifesto; he withheld judgment and left only the act itself, and the history of Urdu literature explains his break from the progressive camp along this axis of contrast.

There is no record of direct contact between the two. This map places them close together because their short-story form overlaps: each cuts the massacres of civil war and partition into scenes only a few pages long, attaches neither commentary nor consolation, and leaves judgment to the reader.

There is no record of direct contact between the two. This map sets them facing each other to show opposite directions: both took the villages and small towns of colonial India as their stage in the same period, but Premchand described a society in need of reform while Narayan described a recurring everyday life.

There is no record of direct contact between the two. This map places them close together because their methods overlap: each invented a fictional place — Yoknapatawpha County and Malgudi — and wrote the same setting and the same characters over and over for decades.

There is no record of direct contact between the two. This map places Land beside War and Peace because their design as sweeping multigenerational novels overlaps: both follow several generations of a single family, letting war and political upheaval pass through them.
